nodes.label: Theorem
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
Put $c_1=0$ and $c_{r+1}=F(c_r)$, where
\[
 F(c)=\frac{(1+c)^2}{8(1-c)}.
\]
For all $n\geq1$, all finite $d$, all orthogonal projections
$P_1,\ldots,P_n$ and all density matrices $\rho$,
\[
 -c_n\leq\mu_n\leq1.
\]
The lower bound is attained in dimension $n$ by real codimension-one
projections and a pure state; for $n=1$ the zero projection suffices.
Furthermore $0\leq c_n<1/3$, $c_n\uparrow1/3$, and
\[
 c_2=\frac18,\qquad c_3=\frac{81}{448},\qquad
 c_4=\frac{279841}{1315328},\qquad
 \frac13-c_n\sim\frac{16}{27n}.
\]
Consequently the uniform infimum is $-1/3$, not attained at any finite
length. The upper bound $1$ is attained.

nodes.statement:
Let $k\geq1$, $r=6k+4$, and $G=\Th_{3,3,r}$. Then $G$ is connected and
twin-free, $|V(G)|=r+5$, and
\[
 \dim(G)=\mm_L(G)=2,\qquad \mm_Q(G)=1.
\]
More precisely, the eigenvalues $1$ and $3$ of $L$ each have multiplicity
two and all other eigenvalues of $L$ are simple; every eigenvalue of $Q$
is simple. Consequently these graphs answer Problem 30 in the
Laplacian-equality direction.

nodes.statement:
For every integer $r\geq6$, $\Th_{3,3,r}$ is connected and twin-free with
metric dimension two. Its repeated eigenvalues are exactly those in the
following table; each listed eigenvalue has multiplicity two, and every
other eigenvalue is simple.
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc|cc}
 r\bmod6&\text{repeated in }L&\text{repeated in }Q&\mm_L&\mm_Q\\\hline
 0&3&1&2&2\\
 1&3&3&2&2\\
 2&\varnothing&\varnothing&1&1\\
 3&1,3&1,3&2&2\\
 4&1,3&\varnothing&2&1\\
 5&\varnothing&\varnothing&1&1
\end{array}
\]
Thus within this subfamily, both equalities hold in residues $0,1,3$;
neither holds in residues $2,5$; and only the Laplacian equality holds
in residue $4$.

nodes.statement:
The graphs $\Th_{3,3,r}$ are connected and twin-free for every $r\geq2$.
Their metric dimension is three for $r=3,5$, and two otherwise.
The spectral table in Corollary~\ref{cor:all-lengths} holds for every
$r\geq3$. For $r=2$, the only repeated Laplacian eigenvalues are
$3-\sqrt2,3+\sqrt2$, both double, and the signless spectrum is simple.
Consequently exactly one equality holds precisely when
\[
 r=2\quad\hbox{or}\quad r\equiv4\pmod6,
\]
and in every such case it is the Laplacian equality.
Both equalities hold precisely for $r\geq6$ with $r\equiv0,1,3\pmod6$.
Neither holds in the other cases. In particular, no graph of this
entire subfamily separates in the signless-equality direction.

nodes.statement:
For $m\ge2$, precisely one partition of $2^m+1$ has each length in
$[m-R_m,m+2]$, and no other length occurs. Thus the full length
distribution is flat, symmetric and unimodal. For every modulus $d\ge1$,

$((R_m+3)^2-1)/12$.

$s(2n+1)=s(n)+s(n+1)$ for $n\ge1$, and put $d(n)=s(n)-a(n)$.

$z\ge1$ zero digits the deficit is $z-1-R_{z+1}$.

nodes.statement:
Let $A_\rho(n)$ count positive halving chains starting from the virtual
predecessor $n$ with total $n+\rho$, as in \cite[Section~4]{alekseyev}.
For $m\ge2$ and $\rho\ge0$,
\[
 A_\rho(2^m+1)=1+\min(m,\rho+2)
                  +\#\{r\ge1:T_r+\rho\le m\}.
\]
In particular, for $m\ge3$ these counts first remain equal to $m+1$
at offset $\rho=m-2$, agreeing with the source's exact threshold
\cite[Theorem~17, Corollary~18]{alekseyev}.

nodes.statement:
Let $a\ne1$ have order $d$ in a finite group $G$ of order $n$.
For $0\leq k\leq n$, let $A_{a,k}$ contain $k$ copies of $a$ and
$n-k$ copies of $1$. Then
\[
 A_{a,k}\text{ is quotient-realizable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d\mid k.
\]
In contrast, its abelianization condition is
$\operatorname{ord}(\pi(a))\mid k$.
If $d\mid k$, exactly $\binom{n/d}{k/d}$ permutations $\phi$ of $G$
have these quotient labels; otherwise there are none.

nodes.statement:
Let $u\ne v$ belong to a finite group $G$ of order $n$.
The multiset with $n-k$ copies of $u$ and $k$ copies of $v$, where
$0\leq k\leq n$, is quotient-realizable if and only if
\[
 \operatorname{ord}(u^{-1}v)\mid k.
\]
Its abelianization condition is exactly
$\operatorname{ord}(\pi(u^{-1}v))\mid k$.
Writing $d=\operatorname{ord}(u^{-1}v)$, the number of realizing
permutations is $\binom{n/d}{k/d}$ when $d\mid k$, and zero otherwise.

nodes.statement:
Let $H_1,\ldots,H_r$ be vertex-disjoint finite simple graphs, each with
specified vertices $v_i,w_i$ satisfying $N_{H_i}(w_i)=\{v_i\}$.
Let $F$ be any simple graph on $\{1,\ldots,r\}$.
Obtain $J_F$ from their disjoint union by adding $v_iv_j$ for each
$ij\in E(F)$. Then
\begin{equation}
 \Dom(J_F)=\{S_1\cup\cdots\cup S_r:S_i\in\Dom(H_i)\},\qquad
 D(J_F,x)=\prod_{i=1}^rD(H_i,x).
\end{equation}
If every $H_i$ and $F$ are connected, then $J_F$ is connected.

nodes.label: Proposition
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
Let $n,r\ge1$ be integers, write $n=\prod_{p\mid n}p^{e_p}$, and set
\[
 D_r(n)=\prod_{p\mid n}p^{\lceil e_p/r\rceil},\qquad
 C_r(n)=\frac{n}{D_r(n)}.
\]
For every integer $s$,
\begin{align}
 \sum_{k=s+1}^{s+n}\left(
 \floor{\frac{k^r}{n}}-\floor{\frac{k^r-1}{n}}\right)&=C_r(n),
 \\
 \prod_{k=s+1}^{s+n}\left(1-2\left(
 \floor{\frac{k^r}{n}}-\floor{\frac{k^r-1}{n}}\right)\right)
 &=(-1)^{C_r(n)}.
\end{align}
For $n>1$, the equality $C_r(n)=n/\rad(n)$ holds exactly when
$r\ge\max_{p\mid n}e_p$; for $n=1$ it holds for every $r\ge1$.
For every $r\ge2$, the product in~\eqref{eq:product-general} equals
$a(n+1)$, independently of $s$.

nodes.statement:
For $p=2$, $s=3$, \eqref{eq:ratio} is
\[
 Q(n)=\frac{\sum_{d\mid n}d^3}{\sum_{e\mid n,\ e\text{ odd}}e^3}
     =\frac{8^{v+1}-1}{7}.
\]
This is A318935, introduced by N. J. A. Sloane on 14 September 2018
as the sum of cubes of the powers of two dividing $n$; Chai Wah Wu gave
its valuation formula that day. Amiram Eldar recorded the equivalent
cubic divisor ratio on 29 October 2026 \cite{cubic}.
The underlying cubic power sum already occurs as $T$ on page~102 of
Lamont's 1982 paper on Cayley integers \cite{lamont}.
It is also a direct weighted consequence:
\[
 Q(n)=1+4\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\d>1}}m(d)\varphi(d)^3.
\]

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
For $N\geq1$, the number of inputs $n\leq N$ with
$H(n)=4\cdot2^k-3$ is
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{N}{2^k}\right\rfloor-
 \left\lfloor\frac{N}{2^{k+1}}\right\rfloor\quad(k\geq0).
\]
Furthermore,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{n=1}^N H(n)=N+4\sum_{j\geq1}2^{j-1}
                    \left\lfloor\frac{N}{2^j}\right\rfloor .
\end{equation}
Among the $2^{\ell-1}$ inputs of binary length $\ell\geq1$, the mean
time is $2\ell-1$ and the maximum is $2^{\ell+1}-3$.
The maximum reproduces Wolfram's earlier closed form \cite{wolfram}; the
distribution and mean follow from the individual-input formula above.

nodes.statement:
For every integer $r\geq1$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{d\mid n}m(d)^r\mu(d)=1-2^r\mathbf{1}_{2\mid n}.
\end{equation}
Using $w(d)=(-1)^{d+1}\mu(d)$ instead gives
\[
 \sum_{d\mid n}(-1)^{d+1}m(d)^r\mu(d)
 =1+2^r\mathbf{1}_{2\mid n}.
\]
This is the general formula in Bala's A010684 block of 22 September 2026.
Its case $r=1$, and also the expression
\[
 (-1)^{n+1}\sum_{d\mid n}m(d)^2\mu(d),
\]
equal $1$ for odd $n$ and $3$ for even $n$.
That block explicitly uses offset 1: in the entry's usual offset-0
notation these expressions are A010684$(n-1)$, whereas
$H_{3197}(n)$ is A010684$(n)$ \cite{comparisons}.

nodes.statement:
Let $B$ be an integer $L\times L$ matrix whose reduction modulo $p$ is
the operator $P(x)\,d/dx$ on $\FF_p[x]/(x^L)$, where $P(0)=1$.
Put $U=p^{2r-1}$ and $T=p^{2r-2}(p-1)^2$. Then
\begin{equation}
 B^U(B^T-I)\equiv0\pmod{p^r}.
\end{equation}
Consequently $B^{j+T}\equiv B^j\pmod{p^r}$ for every $j\geq U$.

nodes.statement:
For $n\ge1$, put $r=\lceil n/2\rceil$ and $s=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$.
Then
\[
a_\sigma(n)=\alpha(n)+p_nq_n+p_{-n}q_{-n},\qquad
\alpha(n)\le a_\sigma(n)\le a(n).
\]
Both bounds hold for every $n\ge0$, simultaneously, with the lower
bound attained by tcd and the upper bound by tea. The balls satisfy
$\beta(n)\le b_\sigma(n)\le b(n)$. In particular,
\[
a(n)-\alpha(n)=\left\lfloor\frac{n^2}{8}\right\rfloor,
\qquad
b(n)-\beta(n)=\sum_{m=1}^n\left\lfloor\frac{m^2}{8}\right\rfloor.
\]
For $n\ge1$, equality in the lower sphere bound holds exactly when
$p_nq_n=p_{-n}q_{-n}=0$. Equality in the upper bound holds exactly when
$|p_n-q_n|\le1$ and $|p_{-n}-q_{-n}|\le1$.

Let a monic real polynomial $p$ have distinct roots, a root $R>1$,
and all its other roots of modulus at most one. If a real sequence
obeys the recurrence with characteristic polynomial $p$, with additive

satisfies $e_j=O(b_j^{1/2})$, then
$b_j=L R^j+O(R^{j/2})$.

nodes.statement:
Let $m=2$ or $3$ and start with nondecreasing nonnegative integer data
$x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}$. Define
\[
 x_{n+m}=\operatorname{round}\sqrt{\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}x_{n+i}^2}.
\]

If $R_m$ is the positive root above one of
$p_m(y)=y^m-y^{m-1}-\cdots-y-1$, then for some $C>0$,
\[
 x_n=C R_m^{n/2}+O(1),\qquad
 \frac{x_{n+1}}{x_n}=\sqrt{R_m}+O(R_m^{-n/2}).
\]

and A400644, revision 28, COMMENTS, hold for their specified initial
data: $\sqrt{(1+\sqrt5)/2}$ and the square root of the tribonacci
constant, respectively.

nodes.statement:
Let $X=\{a_i/1000:0\leq i\leq7\}\subset\mathbb R^4$ with ordinary
Euclidean distance, and $Z_{ij}=\exp(-D_{ij}/1000)$.
Every nonempty principal submatrix of $Z$ is positive definite.
Deletion removes exactly indices $6,7$ at its first step and stops at
the second solve, with probability $p$ supported on $\{0,\ldots,5\}$.
For $p'=(999/1000)p+(1/1000)e_6$,
\[
 \frac{57}{10^9}< E(p)-E(p') <\frac{59}{10^9}.
\]
Thus the Euclidean part of Bouafia's Open problem has answer no.

nodes.statement:
For every real $m>0$ and every real $r\geq4$,
\[
 \frac{M_n(m)}{(m+1)^n}\longrightarrow\frac{2}{m(m+1)},\qquad
 \frac{M_n(-r)}{(r-1)^n}\longrightarrow\frac{2}{r(r-1)}.
\]
At step $-3$, instead,
\[
 \frac{M_n(-3)}{5^{n/2}}\longrightarrow\frac1{\sqrt{45}},\qquad
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log M_n(-3)}n=\tfrac12\log5.
\]
In particular, $M_n(-4)/3^n\to1/6$ and
$M_n(-5)/4^n\to1/10$, whereas $M_n(-3)/2^n\to\infty$.
The proposed growth invariance between steps $1$ and $-3$ fails.
nodes.title: Proof of Chen and Chen's parity-positivity conjectures: OEIS A392664–A392666, COMMENTS, and Conjecture 2 (p. 1)

nodes.statement:
For $q\geq1$, the two excluded integer steps satisfy
\[
 R_{-1,2q}(y)=R_{-2,2q}(y)=(1-y)^{2q-2}(1+y),
\]
and
\[
 R_{-1,2q+1}(y)=(1-y)^{2q-2}(1+y^2),\qquad
 R_{-2,2q+1}(y)=(1-y)^{2q}.
\]
Thus $M_n(-1)=M_n(-2)=1$ for $n\geq2$; both growth exponents
are zero. Also $R_{0,n}=(1+y)^{n-1}$. For $m>0$ and $n\geq2$,
every root of $R_{m,n}$ is simple and negative. At $m=-3$,
nonreal roots occur already in row 6.

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
Writing $y=x(t-1)$, one has
\begin{align}
 \sum_{n\geq0}R_n(t)z^n
 &=\frac{t}{(1+z)(\exp(-z/(1+z))-t)},\\
 G(x,t)&=\frac{t-1}{(1-y)(t-\exp(y/(1-y)))}.
\end{align}
Let $s_j=\mathrm{A000262}(j)$, characterized by
$\sum s_j u^j/j!=\exp(u/(1-u))$. Then the modified Riordan recurrence
stated in A131758 is
\begin{equation}
 P_n(t)=n!(t-1)^n+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom nj s_{n-j}
 (t-1)^{n-j-1}P_j(t)\quad(n\geq1).
\end{equation}
If $E_n(t)$ denotes the Eulerian polynomial normalized by
$\sum_{v\geq1}v^n t^v=tE_n(t)/(1-t)^{n+1}$, including $E_0=1$, then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{E_n(t)}{n!}=\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj(1-t)^{n-j}\frac{P_j(t)}{j!}.
\end{equation}
The inverse replaces $E_n$ on the left by $P_n$, and $P_j$ on the right
by $E_j$ and $(1-t)^{n-j}$ by $(t-1)^{n-j}$. In particular the
alternating row sum is
\[
 P_n(-1)=n!\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj(-2)^{n-j}\frac{E_j(-1)}{j!}.
\]
nodes.title: Exact contents in Copeland's polynomial-content conjecture via Carlitz's congruence

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
Let $A_n(t)$ be the row polynomials of A131202, including $A_0=1$,
with the generating function specified in that entry \cite{related}.
Then
\begin{equation}
 A_n(t)=P_n(t)-n(t-1)P_{n-1}(t)\quad(n\geq1),\qquad
 P_n(t)=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk A_{n-k}(t)k!(t-1)^k.
\end{equation}
Consequently the multiplier sequence in its reconstruction of $P_n$
is $k!(t-1)^k$, rather than the printed
``c(n,t) = n!*(t-1)\^{}(n-1) for n > 0''.
At $n=1$ the printed rule gives $2$, whereas $P_1(t)=t$.
At $t=2$ the identity is $A_n(2)=P_n(2)-nP_{n-1}(2)$, as stated in
A084358. The binomial matrix with entries
$\binom nk A_{n-k}(2)$ is A133289 and its inverse is $2I-$A129652.
Also $A_n(1)=n!$, and $A_n(t)$ has degree $n-1$ and leading
coefficient $s_n$ for $n\geq1$, as stated in A131202.

nodes.statement:
For full identity-weight ONB tomography of a full-rank state, let $\CM$
denote the optimal individual-measurement cost, as in \cite[Eq.~(3)]{Das}.
Then
\[
 \CN\leq\CM\leq d^2+d-1-P,\qquad
 \frac{\CM}{\CH}\leq F_d(P)\leq d+1.
\]
The maximum ratio is $d+1$, attained exactly at $\rho=\Id_d/d$.
No existence assumption for SIC POVMs is needed.
The Gill--Massar ratio $C_{\mathrm{GM}}/\CH$ has the same upper envelope
$F_d(P)$ and the same unique maximizer.

nodes.statement:
Let $U_1=\N\setminus\{1\}$. Among all proper numerical semigroups,
\[
 \Phi(S)=U_1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 S=O_m:=\{0\}\cup\{n\in\N:n\geq m\}\quad\text{for some }m\geq2.

exactly one source of each positive Frobenius number.

nodes.label: Corollary

nodes.statement:
For the family in Eq.~(13) and Fig.~4(b) of~\cite{DSS},
\[
 \omega_p=p|\Psi^-\rangle\langle\Psi^-|+(1-p)|00\rangle\langle00|,
 \qquad |\Psi^-\rangle=(|01\rangle-|10\rangle)/\sqrt2,
\]
the full one-sided optimum is
\begin{equation}
 \HF{A}(\omega_p)=\HF{B}(\omega_p)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&0\leq p\leq1/2,\\[2pt]
 \displaystyle\sqrt{1+\frac{2(2p-1)^2}{-3p^2+6p-2}},
       &1/2<p\leq1.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
For every $p>0$, the two-sided filtered supremum is $\sqrt3$.
In particular, $0<p\leq1/2$ gives locally AB-inaccessible maximal
hidden $\F$ violation, with ``maximal'' interpreted as a supremum.
For normalized CHSH, one-sided violation occurs exactly for $p>2/3$;
the two-sided supremum is $\sqrt2$ for every $p>0$.
The unfiltered transitions are $p>2/3$ for $\F$ and $p>1/\sqrt2$
for CHSH.

nodes.statement:
For the asymmetric state
$\mu_{\theta,p}=p|\phi_\theta\rangle\langle\phi_\theta|
+(1-p)\rho_A\otimes\id/2$, $0\leq p\leq1$,
\[
 c_B=0,\quad c_A=\frac{z(1-p^2)}{1-p^2z^2},\quad
 \HF{A}(\mu_{\theta,p})=\sqrt3p,\quad
 \mathrm{HB}_A(\mu_{\theta,p})=\sqrt2p.
\]
Consequently $p>1/\sqrt3$ and $c_A\geq2/3$ certify
Alice-accessible, Bob-inaccessible hidden $\F$ violation.
This region is nonempty for each $1/\sqrt3<p<1$ and sufficiently
small positive $\theta$.
Likewise $p>1/\sqrt2$ and $c_A\geq1/2$ certify
Alice-accessible, Bob-inaccessible hidden CHSH violation;
this region is nonempty for every $1/\sqrt2<p<1$.

nodes.statement:
For the symmetric state
$\nu_{\theta,p}=p|\phi_\theta\rangle\langle\phi_\theta|
+(1-p)\rho_A\otimes\rho_B$, both centres equal $z(1-p)$.
Put $v=\cos\theta\sin\theta$,
$J=(1-p)v^2$, $C=pv$ and
$H=v\sqrt{p+(1-p)^2v^2}$. If
\begin{equation}
 z(1-p)\geq2/3,\qquad C^2>2HJ,
\end{equation}
then $\nu_{\theta,p}$ has AB-inaccessible hidden $\F$ violation.
For each $0<p<1/3$ these conditions hold at sufficiently small
positive $\theta$. In particular $p=1/4$, $z=99/100$ is an
explicit example.
The analogous sufficient region for AB-inaccessible hidden CHSH
violation is $z(1-p)\geq1/2$ and $C^2>4HJ$.
For every $0<p<1/2$ this region is nonempty at sufficiently small
positive $\theta$.

nodes.statement:
Suppose $k\ge2$ and the least eventual period of
\eqref{eq:recurrence} is four. Then
\[
z(k)-\mu_A(k)=
\begin{cases}9,&k=2,\\6,&k\ge3.\end{cases}
\]
In particular, the restriction of Conjecture~23 to $k\ge3$ is true.
For $k\ge3$, necessarily $k\equiv2,3\pmod4$, and the first
capturing run starts at
\[
s=\begin{cases}
\mu_A(k)-k+4,&k\equiv2\pmod4,\\
\mu_A(k)-k+5,&k\equiv3\pmod4.
\end{cases}
\]
The triple $(x_{\mu_A(k)},x_{\mu_A(k)+1},x_{\mu_A(k)+2})$
is respectively $(2,2,0)$ or $(1,2,0)$.

nodes.statement:

\]

nodes.statement:
Let $d\ge2$ and $s\ge1$ be integers, let $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$,
and put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 Q(x)=x^d(1+\varepsilon x)^s,\quad Q_0(x)=x,\quad Q_{j+1}(x)=Q(Q_j(x)),\\
 P_Q(x)=\prod_{j\ge0}(1+\varepsilon Q_j(x)).
 \end{gathered}
\]
For $t\in\{1,s\}$, the series $U_t(x)=xP_Q(x)^t$ is the unique
series with constant coefficient zero and linear coefficient one satisfying
\begin{equation}
 U_t(Q(x))=x^{d-1}(1+\varepsilon x)^{s-t}U_t(x).
\end{equation}
Its compositional inverse $T_t$ satisfies
\[
 T_t\bigl(x^{d-1}(1+\varepsilon x)^{s-t}U_t(x)\bigr)=Q(x).
\]
When $\varepsilon=1$, both $U_1$ and $U_s$ have radius $r_{d,s}$,
the unique positive solution of $r_{d,s}^{d-1}(1+r_{d,s})^s=1$.

nodes.label: Theorem
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
Let \(S\) be a nonempty finite semigroup and
\(\rho:S\to\operatorname{End}_k(V)\) a multiplicative map, where \(V\) is finite
dimensional over any field. Suppose every \(\rho(s)\) is singular. Put
\(d=\dim V\), \(r_s=\rank\rho(s)\), and \(t=|S|\). Then \(d\geq1\).
For every \(n\geq1\), the diagonal action on \(V^{\otimes n}\) has a finite
indecomposable decomposition, and every such decomposition, with \(b(n)\)
factors, satisfies
\begin{equation}
 d^n-2\sum_{s\in S}r_s^n\ \leq\ \mu(V^{\otimes n})\ \leq\ b(n)\ \leq\ d^n.
\end{equation}
In particular, \(b(n)/d^n\to1\), and a copy of \(Z\) is a direct summand
whenever
\begin{equation}
 n\geq1,\qquad 2\sum_{s\in S}r_s^n<d^n.
\end{equation}
Such an exponent always exists.
nodes.title: Quantitative null tensor summands for He–Tubbenhauer’s Conjecture 4.2 (arXiv:2508.04054v1, p. 17): extending their 2025 theorem

\[

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
Let \(M\) be a finite monoid with unit group \(G\), and let \(V\ne0\) be a
finite-dimensional unital \(kM\)-module. Suppose no element other than \(1\)
acts as the identity and \(|G|\) is invertible in \(k\). Put \(S=M\setminus G\),
\(d=\dim V\) and \(r_s=\rank\rho(s)\). For every \(n\geq1\), there is an
invariant decomposition
\[
 V^{\otimes n}=L_n\oplus U_n,\qquad S L_n=0,
 \qquad \dim U_n\leq2\sum_{s\in S}r_s^n.
\]
Consequently Conjecture~3A.2 holds under these hypotheses. If \(b_M(n)\) and
\(b_G(n)\) count indecomposable summands before and after restriction to \(G\),
then
\begin{equation}
 0\leq b_G(n)-b_M(n)\leq2\sum_{s\in S}r_s^n,
 \qquad b_M(n)/b_G(n)\longrightarrow1.
\end{equation}
When \(G=\{1\}\), over every field,
\(b_M(n)/d^n\to1\); the extra composition-ratio hypothesis of
\cite[Proposition~3C.2, p.~16]{HT25} is unnecessary.
nodes.title: Quantitative null tensor summands for He–Tubbenhauer’s Conjecture 4.2 (arXiv:2508.04054v1, p. 17): extending their 2025 theorem

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
For identity return order and normalized mixed-sign rotors
$c_i^2-\varepsilon_i s_i^2=1$, put $w_i=s_i^2$ and
\[
z_i=1+\varepsilon_iw_i+\mathrm i\varepsilon_iw_i
       =\rho_i e^{\mathrm i\alpha_i},\qquad
\rho_i=\sqrt{(1+\varepsilon_iw_i)^2+w_i^2},
\]
where $\alpha_i=\operatorname{atan2}(\varepsilon_iw_i,1+\varepsilon_iw_i)$.
Then
\begin{equation}
t(\Theta_k(\mathrm{id}))
=\operatorname{Re}\!\left[(1+\mathrm i)\prod_i z_i\right]
=\sqrt2\prod_i\rho_i\,
  \cos\!\left(\frac\pi4+\sum_i\alpha_i\right).
\end{equation}
It vanishes exactly when $\sum_i\alpha_i\in\pi/4+\pi\mathbb Z$.
Zeros exist for some parameters exactly when at least two signs
$\varepsilon_i$ agree. In particular a two-factor opposite-square loop has
scalar part $1+2w_1w_2$ and never vanishes.

nodes.label: Corollary

nodes.statement:
For the square-minus-one formula, let $G_\tau$ be the graph on $I$ with
edge $\{i,j\}$ when $i<j$ and $\tau^{-1}(i)<\tau^{-1}(j)$.
Write $F_\tau(w)=t(\Theta_k(\tau))$ and let $e_\tau(S)$ count the
edges induced by $S$. Then
\begin{equation}
F_\tau(w)=\sum_{S\subseteq I}(-1)^{e_\tau(S)}
       \prod_{i\in S}w_i\prod_{i\notin S}(1-w_i).
\end{equation}
For reverse return order its range is $\{1\}$; for every other order
its range on $[0,1]^k$ is exactly $[-1,1]$, and it has a zero.
It factors across the connected components of $G_\tau$, and cannot
factor across any partition that cuts an edge. In particular it is a
product of single-variable functions exactly for reverse order.

nodes.label: Theorem
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
For every integer $m\geq1$, the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $P_m$ is a rational two-dimensional polytope with $m+4$ edges.
The pointed cone $K_m$ is full-dimensional in $\R^3$ and has $m+4$ facets.
Both sets are polyhedra in the real-half-space convention on $\C^3$.
\item Both sets contain $e=(1,1,1)$ and are closed under the Hadamard product.
\item There is a real invertible matrix $S_0$ with
$P_m\subset\mathcal P(S_0)$ and $K_m\subset\mathcal C(S_0)$; the
realizing matrices can all be chosen symmetric.
\item For every $S\in\operatorname{GL}_3(\C)$,
$P_m\ne\mathcal P(S)$ and $K_m\ne\mathcal C(S)$.
\end{enumerate}

\[

                        \ 0\leq z_i\leq1\},\qquad

nodes.label: Theorem
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
For every $n\geq1$ and $x\in\R_{\geq0}^n$,
\[
 \Dstar(x)=P(x).
\]
Every complete greedy history attains this value, independently of all
tie choices. More generally, if $x^{(0)}=x$ and
$x^{(s+1)}=T_{i_s}x^{(s)}$ describe any complete history, then
\begin{equation}
 C_H(x)-P(x)=\sum_{s=0}^{n-2}\delta_{i_s}(x^{(s)}),
 \qquad \delta_i(x)\geq0,
\end{equation}
where, writing $a=x_i$, $b=x_{i+1}$ and $m=\max(a,b)$,
\begin{align}
\delta_i(x)={}&
\begin{cases}
 \max(x_{i-1},m)-\max(x_{i-1},a),& i>1,\\
 0,&i=1
\end{cases}\notag\\
&+\begin{cases}
 \max(m,x_{i+2})-\max(b,x_{i+2}),&i+1<n,\\
 0,&i+1=n.
\end{cases}
\end{align}
Consequently, a history is optimal if and only if every one of its

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
Two bipartite graphs with two inputs and $n$ outputs are equivalent if
and only if they have the same $z$ and the same unordered triple
$\{a,b,c\}$, with multiplicities retained. Over all equivalent bipartite
forms, the minimum number of shared outputs is
\[
 m=\min(a,b,c)\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n-z}{3}\right\rfloor.
\]
The minimum total number of edges is $n-z+m$.
When the row rank is two, the minimum can be attained in a pivot form.
The upper bound is sharp for every $n-z\geq2$.
For two inputs, output cut ranks on singletons and pairs already determine
the row space, with the output labels fixed.

nodes.statement:
The recurrence form of Conjecture 2.16.1 of \cite[p.~73]{critical}
is as follows. Set $p_0=1$ and, for $j\ge0$, define
\[
 p_{j+1}=p_j+3+2\left(\fl{(j+2)/\ph}-\fl{(j+1)/\ph}\right).
\]
The actual orders with three maximum-degree vertices are
$p_1,p_2,\ldots=6,9,14,19,22,\ldots$.
Successive increments are $3$ or $5$, with no consecutive $3$s
and no three consecutive $5$s. The order-one value is a synthetic
seed, not a graph with three maximum-degree vertices.
This is the recurrence reformulation of Patel's prior classification
\cite{patelsets}; the full maximum-set and never-singleton-label
classifications \cite{patelsets,patelnever} are separate results.

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
For $v\geq k\geq1$,
\[
c(v,k)=e_{v-k}(1,\ldots,v-1),\qquad
\sum_{v\geq k}c(v,k)\frac{t^v}{v!}=\frac{(-\log(1-t))^k}{k!}.
\]
For $v\geq0$ there is the polynomial identity
\[
\sum_{k=0}^v c(v,k)b^k x^{v-k}=\prod_{j=0}^{v-1}(b+jx),
\]
which includes all four families of weighted row evaluations listed by
Del\'eham (2007--2008), as well as the row sums $v!$.
For $v>k\geq1$, the two recurrences posed by Kurkov in A132393,
FORMULA (5 March 2025), are
\begin{align*}
(v-k)c(v,k)&=\sum_{j=2}^{v-k+1}\binom{-k}{j}(-1)^j c(v,k+j-1),\\
(v-k)c(v,k)&=\sum_{j=2}^{v-k+1}(j-2)!\binom vj c(v-j+1,k).
\end{align*}
The row identity already appears in the Quaintance--Gould notes (2010),
\S9.3.3, equation (9.20), there attributed to Hagen (1891)~\cite{qg}.
In that notation set $d=v-k$ and replace the summation index $j$ by $v-r$;
the binomial coefficient becomes $\binom r{k-1}$.
The column recurrence has Petrov's proof of 1 March 2025;
ploosu2 proved both by generating functions on 10 August 2025~\cite{recurrences}.
Lee gave combinatorial proofs of both in 2026~\cite[Theorems 11 and 14]{lee}.
For $v\geq1$ the weighted row sums are
\begin{gather*}
\sum_k k c(v,k)=v!H_v,\qquad
\sum_k(k\mathbin{\pm}1)c(v,k)=v!(H_v\mathbin{\pm}1),\\
\sum_k k c(v,v-k)=v!(v-H_v).
\end{gather*}
These give the first four Heinz formulas of 2 July 2026 in A132393.
In order, the sequence identifications are A000254 at $v$;
A000774 at $v$; A001705 at $v-1$; and A067318 at $v$~\cite{weighted}.

nodes.label: Corollary

nodes.statement:
Let $C(x)=\sum_{r\ge0}C_rx^r$ and
$G(t,x)=\sum_{k\ge0}P_k(t)x^k$. In $\ZZ[t][[x]]$,
\begin{equation}
 G(t,x)=\frac{C(tx)}{1-xC(tx)},\qquad
 1+xG(t,x)=\frac1{1-xC(tx)}.
\end{equation}
If $U=xG(t,x)$, then
\[
 x=\frac{U(1-(t-1)U)}{(1+U)^2}.
\]
Thus $U$ is the compositional inverse of
$y(1-(t-1)y)/(1+y)^2$. Also $1+xG$ is the formal continued fraction
with first numerator $x$ and every subsequent numerator $tx$,
all subtracted from unit denominators.

nodes.statement:
Let $A,B\in\CC^{p\times n}$, where $p,n\geq1$, and put
\[
 H=A^*B+B^*A,\qquad R=A^*A+B^*B.
\]
For every $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$,
\begin{equation}
 |\det H[S,S]|\leq\det R[S,S].
\end{equation}
Consequently, for $0\leq k\leq n$,
\begin{equation}
 \bigl|\ee_k(\lambda(H))\bigr|
 \leq\sum_{|S|=k}|\det H[S,S]|
 \leq\ee_k(\lambda(R)).
\end{equation}

With $T(1-pT)^r=z$ and $T(0)=0$, the following identities hold:
\begin{align}
 e_n&=[x^n]\Phi(x)^n
 =\sum_{k=0}^np^k(-v)^{n-k}\binom{(r+1)n}{k},\\
 E_r(z)&=\sum_{n\geq0}e_nz^n
 =\frac{1-pT}{(1-qT)(1-(r+1)pT)},\\
 \exp\left(\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{e_n}{n}z^n\right)
 &=\frac{R(z)}z=\frac{1}{(1-qT)(1-pT)^r},
 \quad R=z\Phi(R).
\end{align}
The coefficients of $R/z$ are integers if $u,v$ are integers.
For $n\geq1$ and $q\ne0$, $p/q\ne1$, the hypergeometric identity is
\begin{multline}
 e_n=q^n(1-p/q)^{-rn}\\
 -p^n\binom{(r+1)n-1}{n}
 \left({}_2F_1(1,(r+1)n;n+1;p/q)-1\right).
\end{multline}
The hypergeometric function here is a rational function of its argument,
continued from its series at zero.

Let $\mathbb K=\R$ or $\C$, let $1\le k$, $1\le r$, and $k+r\le n$.
Let $z_1,\ldots,z_r$ be orthonormal, set
$V=\operatorname{span}(z_1,\ldots,z_r)^\perp$, and take any

 \sum_{T\in\binom{[n]}{k+r}}\left(\min_{\substack{S\subset T\\|S|=k}}a_S\right)|b_T|^2
 \ \le\ \sum_{S\in\binom{[n]}k}a_S|u_S|^2
 \ \le\ \sum_{T\in\binom{[n]}{k+r}}\left(\max_{\substack{S\subset T\\|S|=k}}a_S\right)|b_T|^2.
\end{equation}

nodes.statement:
Let $h(t)=(3t-t^3)/2$ on $[0,1]$. It is strictly increasing,
$h(1)=1$, and $h(t)/t=(3-t^2)/2$ is strictly decreasing for $0<t\le1$.
Over nonnegative unit vectors of arbitrary finite dimension,
\begin{equation}
\inf R_h(x)^2=\frac{16(17-9\sqrt3)}{23}.
\end{equation}
The infimum is not attained in a finite dimension. Restricting to at most
two nonzero coordinates gives the attained minimum $80/81$ instead.
For example, a vector with squared coordinates $(4/5,1/10,1/10)$ gives
\[
R_h(x)^2=\frac{13689}{13885}<\frac{80}{81}.
\]
The infimum in~\eqref{eq:sphereinf} is approached by one squared coordinate
$a_*=6-3\sqrt3$ and $m$ squared coordinates $(1-a_*)/m$ as $m\to\infty$.

nodes.statement:
Fix $z>0$ and either the Cartesian grid family or the king graph family
$P_m\boxtimes P_n$. Within the chosen family, the free rectangles,
their one-direction periodic versions, and their two-direction periodic
versions have a common joint logarithmic rate $h(z)$, depending on the
family. The king adjacency
means that distinct vertices differ by at most one in each coordinate;
periodic versions use the corresponding cyclic coordinate distance.
If $F_{a,b}(z)=\log Z_{a,b}(z)/(ab)$ for free rectangles, then
\begin{equation}
 h(z)=\sup_{a,b\ge1}F_{a,b}(z),\qquad
 0\le h(z)-F_{a,b}(z)
 \le 2\log\kappa_z\left(\frac1a+\frac1b\right).
\end{equation}
The finite periodic/free ratios are at most $\kappa_z^{2n}$ for one
seam and $\kappa_z^{2(m+n)}$ for two seams.

nodes.statement:
In a fragment with $n$ centres and imbalance $d$, all eigenvalues are
\begin{equation}

                         +\frac\Delta2d,

$\Delta=2/\sqrt7$ give 56 zero modes in an imbalanced fragment.

nodes.statement:
Let $u,v$ have weight $n\ge1$. If their hikes differ, $N^*_{u,v}=0$.
If their common hike is zero, $u=v=1^n$ and $N^*_{u,v}=1$.
For common hike $p\ge1$, write $a=\sigma(u)$ and $b=\sigma(v)$.
Then
\[
 N^*_{u,v}>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 a_i\ge b_i\quad(2\le i\le p+1).
 \tag{9}
\]
For a supported pair its unique composition is
\begin{align}
 \kappa_1&=a_1,\notag\\
 \kappa_{2j}&=b_{j+1}-1,\qquad
 \kappa_{2j+1}=a_{j+1}-b_{j+1}+1\quad(1\le j<p),\notag\\
 \kappa_{2p}&=b_{p+1},
 \tag{10}
\end{align}
followed by $\kappa_{2p+1}=a_{p+1}-b_{p+1}$ exactly when this
difference is positive. Its entry is given by (2).

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
The following descriptions hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $c_e(n)$ counts primes $p$ with $p^e\le n$, and prime factors
whose exponent in $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,n)$ is at least $e$.
For $e=2$ it also counts positive integers at most $n$ with exactly
three divisors, and is the maximum size of a pairwise coprime collection
of composite integers at most $n$.
\item For $e\ge1$, $c_e(n)=j$ exactly when
$p_j^e\le n<p_{j+1}^e$, with the $j=0$ interval $1\le n<2^e$.
As formal power series,
\[
 \sum_{n\ge1}c_e(n)x^n=\frac{\sum_{p\in\pr}x^{p^e}}{1-x}.
\]
In particular,
\[
 \sum_{n\ge1}a(n)x^n
 =\frac{\sum_{p\in\pr}x^{p^3}}{1-x}
   +x^2+x^3+x^6+x^7+x^2\sum_{j=0}^{8}x^{3j}.
\]
\item For fixed $e$, the prime number theorem gives
$c_e(n)\sim e n^{1/e}/\log n$ as $n\to\infty$. In particular,
$a(n)\sim3n^{1/3}/\log n$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.title: Exact counts and sharp growth for OEIS A222759, first comment (12 March 2013): extending Glaisher (1900)

nodes.statement:
Let $G(1)=1$, $G(x+1)=\Gamma(x)G(x)$ be the Barnes $G$-function,
and let $A$ be the Glaisher--Kinkelin constant. For $n\ge0$,
\[
b_n=\frac{\sqrt{G(2n+2)}}{2^{n^2/2}G(n+1)\sqrt{\Gamma(n+1)}}.
\]
The equivalent half-integer formula recorded by Reshetnikov (6 November 2015) is
\[
 b_n=2^{n(n+1)/2-1/24}A^{3/2}\pi^{-n/2-1/4}e^{-1/8}G(n+3/2).
\]
As $n\to\infty$,
\begin{align*}
 b_n&\sim\frac{A^{1/2}2^{n^2/2+n+5/24}
 n^{n^2/2+n/2+1/24}}{\exp(3n^2/4+n/2+1/24)},\\
 a_n&\sim\frac{A^{1/2}2^{n^2+n/2+5/24}
 n^{n^2/2+n/2+1/24}}{\exp(3n^2/4+n/2+1/24)}.
\end{align*}
These are the Barnes formula and asymptotics recorded by Kotesovec in
A057863 (8 April 2021; 13 November 2014) and A086205 (11 July 2015).

nodes.statement:
Let $U(N,d)=\C_d(\lfloor N/d\rfloor)$ for $1\leq d\leq N$,
the triangle A400203, revision 17, FORMULA \cite{a400203}.
Then
\begin{equation}
 U(N,d)=\sum_{\substack{q\leq N/d\\\rad(q)\mid d}}
                  M(\lfloor N/(dq)\rfloor).
\end{equation}
Its boundary and plateau formulas are
\[
 U(N,1)=M(N),\quad U(N,d)=1\ (2d>N),\quad
 U(N,d)=U(d\lfloor N/d\rfloor,d).
\]
For $1\leq d<N$, its increment is $\mob(N/d)$ when
$d\mid N$ and $(N/d,d)=1$, and zero otherwise.
Writing $H(k)=1$ if every prime exponent of $k$ is at least two,
and $H(k)=0$ otherwise, with $H(1)=1$, gives
\begin{align}
 \sum_{d=1}^{N}U(N,d)&=\sum_{k=1}^{N}H(k)
                         =\mathrm{A217038}(N+1),\\
 \sum_{d=1}^{N}\mob(d)U(N,d)&=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mob(k)\tau(k)
                         =\mathrm{A062563}(N),\\
 \sum_{d=1}^{N}\mob(d)^2U(N,d)&=1.
\end{align}
Here $H$ is A112526, $\tau(k)$ is the number of positive divisors,
and A217038 counts powerful numbers strictly below its argument
\cite{triangle-aux}.

nodes.statement:
Write $s(d)=\sum_{k\leq d,(k,d)=1}\mob(k)^2$ (A073311 \cite{a073311}).
The formulas and data of A304575 \cite{a304575} give the sequence
\begin{equation}
 R(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}s(d)
 =\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mob\!\left(\frac{k}{(k,n)}\right)^2
 =\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mob\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(n,k)}{n}\right)^2.
\end{equation}
Consequently $R(n)\leq n$ and
$s(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mob(n/d)R(d)$.
If the strict inequality $k<d$ in that entry's NAME is read literally
for positive $k$, its divisor sum equals $R(n)-1$, not $R(n)$.
For $Q(t)=\sum_{1\leq k<t}\mob(k)^2$ (A013928 \cite{a013928}),
every prime $p$ and integer $m\geq0$ satisfy
\begin{align}
 R(p^{2m})&=1+\sum_{i=0}^{m}Q(p^{2i}),\\
 R(p^{2m+1})&=1+\sum_{i=0}^{m}Q(p^{2i+1}).
\end{align}

nodes.statement:
For every $n\geq1$,
\begin{equation}
 0\leq a(n)-F_{2n-1}\leq F_{2\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\leq F_n,
 \qquad
 0\leq \frac{a(n)}{F_{2n-1}}-1\leq\frac1{F_n}.
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 a(n)\sim\frac{\ph^{2n-1}}{\sqrt5},\qquad
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a(n)}{a(n-1)}=\ph^2.
\end{equation}
The ratio is defined for every $n\geq2$. Equivalently, for every
$\epsilon>0$ there is an integer $N\geq2$ such that
$|a(n)/a(n-1)-\ph^2|<\epsilon$ for every integer $n\geq N$.

nodes.statement:
For $n\geq2$,
\[
0\leq R(n)-\eta_n F_{n-1}\leq F_{2\lfloor n/3\rfloor}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\frac{a(n)}{F_{2n-1}}-1
=\eta_n\ph^{-n}+O(\ph^{-4n/3}),
\]
and
\begin{align*}
\lim_{m\to\infty}\ph^{2m}
 \left(\frac{a(2m)}{a(2m-1)}-\ph^2\right)&=\ph^2,\\
\lim_{m\to\infty}\ph^{2m+1}
 \left(\frac{a(2m+1)}{a(2m)}-\ph^2\right)&=-\ph^3.
\end{align*}
Both $O(\ph^{-n})$ error orders are therefore sharp. The successive
ratios eventually lie above $\ph^2$ at even indices and below it at
odd indices.

nodes.statement:
For $c(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}F_d$, Jovovic's ordinary generating function
and Gutkovskiy's logarithmic identity in A007435 are
\[
 \sum_{n\geq1}c(n)x^n
 =\sum_{j\geq1}\frac{x^j}{1-x^j-x^{2j}},\qquad
 \sum_{n\geq1}\frac{c(n)x^n}{n}
 =-\sum_{j\geq1}\frac{F_j}{j}\log(1-x^j).
\]
For $b_n=F_n$ or $b_n=F_{2n-1}$, and $A(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}b_d$,
the inverse formula is
\[
 b_n=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)A(n/d).
\]
Here $\mu(d)=0$ if $d$ has a squared prime factor, and otherwise is
$(-1)^r$ if $d$ is a product of $r$ distinct primes.

nodes.statement:
Let $d_m=\operatorname{den}(C(m,m+3))$ and $g_m=\gcd(3,m+2)$.
For every $m\ge0$,
\begin{equation}
 C(m,m+3)=\frac{(-1)^{m+1}(2m+1)}{(m+1)(m+2)},\qquad
 d_m=\frac{(m+1)(m+2)}{g_m}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for $k\ge0$,
\begin{align}
 (d_{3k},d_{3k+1},d_{3k+2})
 &=\bigl((3k+1)(3k+2),(k+1)(3k+2),3(k+1)(3k+4)\bigr),\\

 \sum_{m\ge0}d_mz^m
 &=\frac{2(1+z+6z^2+7z^3+2z^4+3z^5+z^6)}{(1-z^3)^3}.
\end{align}
The two shifted-sequence formulas in A194767 also hold:
\[
 d_m=(m+1)\mathrm{A051176}(m+2),\qquad
 d_{m+2}=2\mathrm{A306368}(m)\quad(m\ge0).
\]
Its fourth-diagonal numerator formula requires a shift:
\begin{equation}
 C(m,m+3)=\frac{(-1)^{m+1}\mathrm{A146535}(m+1)}{d_m},
 \quad\text{not }\frac{(-1)^{m+1}\mathrm{A146535}(m)}{d_m}.
\end{equation}

\[

nodes.statement:
For $T_{b,c}(n,k)=[x^k](1+bx+cx^2)^n$,
\begin{align*}
 T_{b,c}(n,k)&=\sum_{\substack{j\geq0\\0\leq k-2j\leq n-j}}
   \binom nj\binom{n-j}{k-2j}b^{k-2j}c^j,\\
 \sum_k T_{b,c}(n,k)&=(1+b+c)^n,\qquad
 \sum_k(-1)^k T_{b,c}(n,k)=(1-b+c)^n,\\
 T_{b,c}(n,2n)&=c^n,\qquad
 T_{b,c}(n,2n-1)=nbc^{n-1}\quad(n\geq1).
\end{align*}
For $b=1$, $c=-m$, the ordinary and alternating row sums are
$(2-m)^n$ and $(-m)^n$. For $b,c\geq0$ the absolute row sum is exactly
$(1+b+c)^n$. Powers with exponent zero have value one, including $0^0$.

$P_m=(x+2)P_{m-1}-P_{m-2}$ for $m\geq2$. Then
\[
[x^k]P_m=b_{m+k+1,k}
=\binom{m+k}{2k}+2\binom{m+k}{2k+1}\quad(0\leq k\leq m).
\]
These are Andr\'e-Jeannin's $r=2$ coefficient theorem (1994,
equation~(9)) and the array A111125 \cite{andre,related-arrays}.

With $P_m$ as above and $z$ invertible,
\[
z^{2m+1}-z^{-(2m+1)}=(z-z^{-1})P_m((z-z^{-1})^2).
\]
Consequently, with the usual Fibonacci numbers $F_n$ and Lucas numbers $L_n$,
\[
P_m(1)=L_{2m+1},\qquad
F_{(2m+1)n}=\sum_{k=0}^m[x^k]P_m(x)\,
(-1)^{(m+k)n}5^kF_n^{2k+1}\quad(n\geq0).
\]
The values $P_m(-1)$ repeat $1,2,1,-1,-2,-1$. For $m\geq1$,
\[
P_m(x)=\prod_{j=1}^m\left(x+4\sin^2\frac{j\pi}{2m+1}\right).
\]
These are established Morgan--Voyce and A111125 identities
\cite{andre,related-arrays}.

nodes.statement:
For $d\geq2$ and $m\geq0$,
\begin{align}
h_d(m)&=\binom{m+d-1}{d-1}+\binom{m+d-2}{d-1}\\
&=2\binom{m+d-1}{d-1}-\binom{m+d-2}{d-2}
=\frac{2m+d-1}{d-1}\binom{m+d-2}{d-2}.\nonumber
\end{align}
Moreover $h_{d+1}(m)=\sum_{j=0}^m h_d(j)$ and
\[
h_d(m)=\sum_{j=1}^d(-1)^{j+1}\binom dj h_d(m-j)\qquad(m\geq d).
\]
As a polynomial in $m$, $h_d$ has degree $d-1$, leading coefficient
$2/(d-1)!$, and symmetry $h_d(-m-d+1)=(-1)^{d-1}h_d(m)$.

nodes.statement:
For $n\geq1$ and $d\geq2$,
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n(-1)^j h_d(j)
\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-j+1)}{(n+d)(n+d+1)\cdots(n+d+j-1)}=0,
\]
where an empty product is $1$. This is Bala's terminating identity (2019)
in A005585, A040977, A050486 and A053347 \cite{columns}.
If $p>d-1$ is prime and $e\geq1$, then $p^e\mid h_d(m)$ whenever
$m+j\equiv0\pmod{p^e}$ for some $1\leq j\leq d-2$, or
$2m+d-1\equiv0\pmod{p^e}$.

nodes.statement:
Let $d\geq4$ and $m\geq0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item In a set $X$ of size $m+d$, take disjoint subsets $Y,Z$ of sizes
$2$ and $m+d-3$. The number of $d$-subsets meeting both is $h_d(m)$.
\item The number of placements of $d-2$ queens on an
$(m+d-2)\times(m+d-2)$ board in distinct rows and columns, with every pair
attacking diagonally, is $2h_d(m)$.
\item For the Chebyshev polynomials $T_0(t)=1$, $T_1(t)=t$,
$T_{j+1}(t)=2tT_j(t)-T_{j-1}(t)$, and $r=d-1$,
\[
[t^r]T_{r+2m}(t)=(-1)^m2^{r-1}h_d(m).
\]
\item The order polytope of a chain of $d-3$ elements below two
incomparable elements has $h_d(m)$ lattice points in its $m$th dilation.
\end{enumerate}

The difference sequence is a concatenation of
$(1,1,1,-3)$ and $(1,1,1,1,-3)$. The first block has length five.
For $j\geq1$, let
\begin{equation}
 R_j=\floor{\frac{j^2+5j+7}{8}}.

Apart from the first block, the blocks of length five have precisely
the block indices $r=R_j$, where the block indexed by $r$ starts at
difference index $n_r$. Their starting indices are $4R_j+j$.
Between the length-five blocks indexed by $R_j$ and $R_{j+1}$ there are
exactly $R_{j+1}-R_j-1=j/4+O(1)$ length-four blocks.

 a(n)=\sqrt{2n}+O(1),\qquad
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a(n)}{\sqrt{2n}}=1.

For every $n\geq0$,
\[
 t(n)=\floor{\frac{2n+5-\sqrt{8n+17}}4},\qquad b(n)=n-2t(n),
 \qquad b(n)=\sqrt{2n}+O(1).
\]
The absolute-mode difference sequence consists of $(1,-1)$ and $(1,1,-1)$.
Its initial block has length three. Apart from that initial block, its
length-three blocks have indices
\[
 L_j=\floor{\frac{(j+1)(j+2)}4},\qquad j\geq1,
\]
and start at difference indices $2L_j+j$.
At every degree with two absolute maxima the two maximizing exponents
are $b(n)$ and $b(n)+2$, their coefficients have opposite signs,
and $B(n)=M(n)$.
More generally, $B(n)=M(n)$ if and only if either there are two absolute
maxima or $t(n)$ is even.
The signed and absolute modes interlace in the precise sense
$a(n)\in\{b(n)-2,b(n),b(n)+2\}$ for every $n\geq0$.

nodes.statement:
Put $C=1/B=\sum_{n\geq0}d_nx^n$ and
$\ell_n=[x^n]xB'/B$ for $n\geq1$. Then
\begin{align}
 b_n&=-\sum_{i=1}^n d_i b_{n-i} &&(n\geq1),\\
 b_n&=-\sum_{i=1}^{n+2}d_i d_{n+2-i} &&(n\geq0),\\
 \ell_n&=[t^n](1-t-t^2)^{-n} &&(n\geq1),\\
 b_n&=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}
 {}_2F_1\!\left(-\frac n2,\frac{1-n}2;-2n;-4\right) &&(n\geq1).
\end{align}
The hypergeometric expression means the finite sum through
$k=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ with summand
$(-n/2)_k((1-n)/2)_k(-4)^k/((-2n)_k k!)$;
$(a)_k=a(a+1)\cdots(a+k-1)$ and $(a)_0=1$.
The coefficients $d_n$ form A217596, and the $\ell_n$ form A213684.

nodes.label: Corollary

nodes.statement:
Let $m,n\geq3$, $z>0$, and let $Z^b_{m,n}(z)$ be the partition
function on the $m\times n$ king board with boundary condition
$b\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{cylinder},\mathrm{torus}\}$. In the
cylindrical case the width $m$ is periodic. Let $P^b_{m,n}(z)$ be its
largest weighted coefficient and put $L=\log(1+z)$. Then
\[
 \frac{\log F_{m,n}(z)}{(m+1)(n+1)}\leq h(z)
 \leq\frac{\log F_{m,n}(z)}{mn},
 \tag{5}
\]
where $F_{m,n}=Z^{\mathrm{free}}_{m,n}$, and
\[
 -\frac{(m+n-1)L+\log(mn+1)}{mn}
 \leq \frac{\log P^b_{m,n}(z)}{mn}-h(z)
 \leq\frac{(m+n+1)L}{mn}.
 \tag{6}
\]
Consequently all three partition functions and their largest weighted
coefficients have entropy $h(z)$ whenever $\min(m,n)\to\infty$,
without a restriction on aspect ratio.

nodes.statement:
Assume~\eqref{fitting} and $\mu\ge3$. Define
\[
 t=b_1-a_\mu,\qquad
 c=\begin{cases}\mu,&a_1>0,\\ \mu-1,&a_1=0,\end{cases}
 \qquad d=\sum_{i=1}^{\mu}a_i(b_i-a_i).
\]
Then $\deg P=d$, $d\ge t+4$, and
\begin{equation}
 \coeff{j}{P}=0\ (j<t+1),\quad
 \coeff{t+1}{P}=1,\quad \coeff{t+2}{P}=c+1,\quad
 \coeff{d-1}{P}=c,\quad \coeff{d}{P}=1.
\end{equation}
In particular, $P$ is not almost palindromic, proving Conjecture 9.63.
The same conclusions hold at width two if
$a_2-a_1\ge2$ and $b_2-b_1\ge2$.

nodes.label: Corollary

nodes.statement:
Let $M(\lambda)$ and $N(\lambda)$ be the sets in Okada's Conjecture 9.64:
$M(\lambda)$ consists of all $0\le a_1<a_2\le b_1<b_2=\lambda$, and
$N(\lambda)$ consists of those tuples whose determinant is not almost
palindromic. For $\lambda\ge2$,
\[
 |M(\lambda)|=\binom{\lambda+1}{3},\quad
 |N(\lambda)|=\binom{\lambda-1}{3},\quad
 |M(\lambda)\setminus N(\lambda)|=(\lambda-1)^2,
\]
where a binomial coefficient with upper index less than three is zero.
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 O(\lambda)=\frac{|N(\lambda)|}{|M(\lambda)|}
           =\frac{(\lambda-2)(\lambda-3)}{\lambda(\lambda+1)}.
\end{equation}
In particular, $O(3)=0$, $O(\lambda+1)>O(\lambda)$ for $\lambda\ge3$,
and $O(\lambda)\longrightarrow1$.

nodes.statement:
Assume~\eqref{fitting} with $\mu\ge2$. For any $\rho\ge1$, put
$G=\deg A_\rho-\deg B_\rho$.
Then
\[
 q^{d_\rho}P_{\rho,G}(q^{-1})=P_{\rho,0}(q).
\]
Hence the zero-shift classification also holds at $e=G$.
If $\mu\ge3$, the determinants at $e=1$ and $e=G-1$ are not almost
palindromic for any $\rho\ge1$.

palindromic. Multiplication by $q^s$ or substitution $q\mapsto q^k$,
for integers $s\ge0$, $k\ge1$, preserves almost palindromicity.

nodes.statement:
For any separable state on $\mathbb C^{d_A}\otimes\mathbb C^{d_B}$,
with $d=\min(d_A,d_B)$ and $D=\max(d_A,d_B)$, its correlation singular
values $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_{d^2}$ satisfy
\[
 \sum_{i=2}^{d^2}s_i
 \le\sqrt{(1-\tr\rho_A^2)(1-\tr\rho_B^2)}
 \le\sqrt{\frac{d-1}{d}\frac{D-1}{D}}.
\]
Equation (D31) in \cite{peled}, arXiv v2, omits the square root on
its last expression and is false as written, even in FNF.

\begin{enumerate}
\item The three gates $A,B,C$ are perfect.
\item The six flattenings of $T$ whose column triples are

nodes.label: Lemma

nodes.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $V=\F_p^n$, and $d=p^n$. Suppose $\Sset$ consists of $d$ symmetric $n\times n$ matrices over $\F_p$, contains zero, and every difference of distinct matrices is invertible. For $M\in\Sset$ and $b\in V$, set
\[
f_{M,b}(x)=x^TMx+b^Tx,\quad
\phi_{M,b}(x)=\frac{2\pi}{p}f_{M,b}(x)\pmod {2\pi},\quad
X(\Sset)=\{\phi_{M,b}:M\in\Sset,\ b\in V\}.
\]
Then $X(\Sset)$ has $d^2$ points, contains zero, is anchored at $x=0$, satisfies \eqref{eq:moment} and \eqref{eq:overlap}, and is a subgroup if and only if $\Sset$ is closed under matrix addition.

nodes.label: Theorem
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
Fix $r\geq3$ and distinct odd primes $q_1,\ldots,q_{r-3}$, with an empty
list when $r=3$. For every integer $K\geq2$, put
\[
 u_{r,K}(n)=1+2^n+2^{Kn}+\sum_{i=1}^{r-3}q_i^n.
\]
This is a positive integer sequence of rank $r$, and its general rank
sequence is
\begin{equation}
 H_{r,K}(M)=\binom{M+r-1}{r-1}-
 \begin{cases}\binom{M-K+r-1}{r-1},&M\geq K,\\0,&M<K.\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Different $K$ give different rank sequences. For $M\geq K$ the displayed
expression is a polynomial of degree $r-2$ with leading coefficient
$K/(r-2)!$.
nodes.title: Infinitely many general rank sequences: extending Patel's polynomiality picture (2026) at arXiv:2501.14643v1, Section 1, p. 2

$\omega^*$-chains. A nonempty countable poset of bounded finite height has a least such extension if
and only if it has a least element.

nodes.statement:
The row sums $U_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}D^+_{n,k}$ and
$L_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}D^-_{n,k}$ are
\begin{align*}
U_n&=\frac{n^2(n+1)(2n+1)+3n(n+\eps)}{12},\\
L_n&=\frac{n^2(n^2+1)}2+T_n-U_n.
\end{align*}
These are the defining formulas of A325517 and A325656
(Spezia, 2019)~\cite{s325517,s325656}. Also
$D^+_{n,n-1}=n$, while $D^-_{n,n-1}$ equals $n^2$ for even $n$
and $n^2-n+1$ for odd $n$, as in A325657~\cite{s325657}.
Writing $Q(z)=(1-z)^5(1+z)^2$, one has
\begin{align*}
\sum_{n\geq0}U_nz^n&=\frac{z(1+3z+7z^2+3z^3+2z^4)}{Q(z)},\\
\sum_{n\geq0}L_nz^n&=\frac{z(1+5z+13z^2+9z^3+4z^4)}{Q(z)},\\
\sum_{n\geq0}L_n\frac{z^n}{n!}
&=\frac{z}{24}\left(3e^{-z}+(21+78z+54z^2+8z^3)e^z\right).
\end{align*}

nodes.label: Corollary

nodes.statement:
Put $h_n=n^2(n^2-1)/12$ and $g_n=n^2(n^2+1)/2$. For $n\geq2$, let
$N^+_{ij}=i+j$ and $N^-_{ij}=i-j$, with $1\leq i,j\leq n$. Then
\[
\det(xI-N^+)=x^{n-2}(x^2-n(n+1)x-h_n),\qquad
\det(xI-N^-)=x^{n-2}(x^2+h_n).
\]
Both matrices have rank two, and
$h_n=\tfrac12\sum_{i,j=1}^n(i-j)^2$ (Bala, 2007, A002415).
The ordinary and exponential generating functions of $h_n$ are
\[
\sum_{n\geq0}h_nz^n=\frac{z^2(1+z)}{(1-z)^5},\qquad
\sum_{n\geq0}h_n\frac{z^n}{n!}
=\frac{e^zz^2(6+6z+z^2)}{12}.
\]
The reciprocal formulas recorded in A002415 and A037270 are
\begin{align*}
\sum_{n\geq2}\frac1{h_n}&=21-2\pi^2,&
\sum_{n\geq2}\frac{(-1)^n}{h_n}&=\pi^2-9,\\
\sum_{n\geq1}\frac1{g_n}&=1+\frac{\pi^2}{3}-\pi\coth\pi,&
\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{g_n}
&=\pi\operatorname{csch}\pi+\frac{\pi^2}{6}-1.
\end{align*}
The nonalternating identities are attributed to Kotesovec (2016 for $h_n$,
2019 for $g_n$), and the alternating ones to Eldar (2020 for $h_n$,
2021 for $g_n$), in those records.

nodes.label: Corollary

nodes.statement:
Put $b(r)=(r-1)(4(r-1)^2+1)$ for $r\geq1$. Its ordinary generating
function, with the source index, and its offset-normalized exponential
generating function are
\[
 \sum_{r\geq1}b(r)x^r=\frac{x^2(5+14x+5x^2)}{(1-x)^4},\qquad
 \sum_{m\geq0}b(m+1)\frac{x^m}{m!}=x(5+12x+4x^2)e^x.
\]
The recurrence is $b(r)=4b(r-1)-6b(r-2)+4b(r-3)-b(r-4)$ for $r\geq5$;
it also holds at $r=4$ with the polynomial extension $b(0)=-5$.
The further descriptions in A317297, COMMENTS and FORMULA (Oktar, 2024;
Navarrete, 2025), follow from
\[
 b(r)=\frac{(2r-1)^4-(2r-3)^4}{16}
     =3\binom{2r-1}{3}+2(r-1).
\]
For $r=1$ the binomial term is zero. The second identity also counts
$b(r)+1$ ternary words of length $L=2r-1$ with exactly one $1$ and
either zero or two $0$'s: choose the $1$ in $L$ ways and the two $0$'s,
if present, in $\binom{L-1}{2}$ ways. Thus the count is
$L+L\binom{L-1}{2}=b(r)+1$. Both polynomial identities follow by expansion.
If $c(j)$ denotes row $j$ of A246696 summed across the row (A246697),
numbered from $0$, then
\[
 c(2m)=4m^3+6m^2+5m+1,\qquad c(2m-1)=4m^3+m\ (m\geq1).
\]
Consequently $b(r)=c(2r-3)$ for $r\geq2$, proving the bisection
conjecture in A317297, CROSSREFS (entry by Pol, 1 September 2018) \cite{trianglelinks}.
These row-sum formulas also prove the equivalent closed-form conjectures
in A246697, FORMULA (Kimberling, 2014; Etienne, 2016; Spezia, 2021).
In full-index form, $c(j)=(2j^3+6j^2+9j+4+j(-1)^j)/4$; hence
\[
 \sum_{j\geq0}c(j)x^j=\frac{1+3x+5x^2+x^3+2x^4}{(1-x)^4(1+x)^2},\quad
 \sum_{j\geq0}c(j)\frac{x^j}{j!}
 =\frac{e^x(2x^3+12x^2+17x+4)-xe^{-x}}4.
\]
This proves its conjectured ordinary and exponential generating functions
(the latter equals the source's hyperbolic expression), and the recurrence
with signature $(2,1,-4,1,2,-1)$ for $j\geq6$.

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
The alternating sum in Sagan--Swanson Conjecture 7.9 satisfies, for $n\ge0$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^{n-k}q^{2(n-k)}\qi{k}!S[n,k]-1
   =(1-q)(1+q)^n-1+q^{n+1}.
\end{equation}
For $n\ge1$ its coefficient at $q^j$, $1\le j\le n$, is
$\binom nj-\binom n{j-1}$; coefficients at zero and $n+1$ vanish.
The nonzero coefficients are positive below $(n+1)/2$, negative above
it, and paired with their negatives by $j\mapsto n+1-j$.
For $n\ge2$, factoring out the initial $q$ makes the absolute-coefficient
polynomial palindromic in the ordinary degree convention.

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
For real $a,t$ define
\[
 w_j(a,t)=\sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor j/3\rfloor}
  \binom j{3r}a^{j-3r}t^r c_r,\qquad
 H_n(a,t)=(w_{i+j}(a,t))_{0\leq i,j\leq n}.
\]
For $t\ne0$, the inertia of $H_n(a,t)$, listed as the numbers of positive,
negative and zero eigenvalues, is
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
n&\operatorname{inertia} H_n(a,t)\\\hline
3m&(2m+1,m,0)\\
3m+1&(2m+1,m,1)\\
3m+2&(2m+2,m+1,0).
\end{array}
\]
In particular, every zero in the original determinant family has nullity
exactly one. For $n\not\equiv1\pmod3$,
\[
 \det H_n(a,t)=t^{n(n+1)/3}W_n.
\]
For $t=0$, the inertia is $(1,0,n)$ and the determinant is $1$ at $n=0$
and $0$ otherwise. For nonzero integers $t$ and $n\not\equiv1\pmod3$,
\[
 \nu_2(\det H_n(a,t))=n+\frac{n(n+1)}3\nu_2(t)
 \quad\text{when }a\in\ZZ.
\]

For every real $\alpha>0$ and integer $n\geq1$, with
$h_j=\sum_{k=1}^j k^{-\alpha}$ and $h_0=0$,
\[
 (-1)^n\det(h_{i+j})_{0\leq i,j\leq n}>0.
\]

order, and also for every positive real order. For order one, a prior
exact evaluation follows from Petrov's answer of February 16, 2017,
Cigler's completion of February 17, and Amdeberhan's independent identity
proof of February 18; see also Cigler, Theorem 4.1, equation (4.2)\cite{harmonic}.

nodes.statement:
Let $B_j$ and $E_j$ denote the Bernoulli and Euler numbers in the
conventions
\[
 \frac{z}{e^z-1}=\sum_{j\geq0}B_j\frac{z^j}{j!},\qquad
 \frac1{\cosh z}=\sum_{j\geq0}E_j\frac{z^j}{j!}.
\]
For every integer $n\geq1$,
\[
 \det(B_{i+j}^2)_{0\leq i,j\leq n}<0,
 \qquad \det(E_{i+j}^2)_{0\leq i,j\leq n}>0.
\]
These are the two assertions of Sun's v5 Conjecture 3.17, p.~18.

nodes.statement:
For a finite group $G$, put $q=|Z(G)|$, $k=k(G)$, and
\[
 I(q)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor q/2\rfloor}
       \frac{q!}{2^j j!(q-2j)!}.
\]
Then
\[
 |\Good(\Conj G)|\le I(q)q^{k-q}.
\]
In particular, $|\Good(\Conj G)|<q^k$ whenever $q\ge2$.
The sharper bound is attained by $G=Q_8$.

nodes.statement:
Let $X=\{\pm i,\pm j\}\subset Q_8$ with its conjugation quandle.
Then $H=\langle X\rangle=Q_8$, $|Z(H)|=2$, $|X/H|=2$, and
\[
 |\Good(\Conj X)|=4
 =\min\bigl(|\Aut(\Conj X)|,\,2^2\bigr),
 \qquad |\Aut(\Conj X)|=8.
\]
Thus Problem 11.7 has a negative answer. Moreover,
$\operatorname{Anti}(\Conj X)=\Aut(\Conj X)\cong C_2\wr S_2$,
and exactly three symmetric-quandle isomorphism classes arise from $X$.

\[

 \begin{cases}10,&n\text{ odd},\\4,&n\text{ even}.\end{cases}

nodes.statement:
The values $A(n,k)$ are integers for all $n,k\in\Nzero$.
For every such $n$ the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every prime $p$, $A(n,p)\equiv-1\pmod p$.
\item For $k\geq1$, $k\ne4$,
\[
 k\mid A(n,k)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k\text{ is not prime}.
\]
At the excluded index, $A(n,4)\equiv2\pmod4$.
\item If $p=2$ or $p\geq7$ is prime, then $A(n,p)/(p-1)$ is an
integer congruent to $1$ modulo $p$ for every $n$.
For $p\in\{3,5\}$, it is an integer if and only if $n$ is even;
whenever it is an integer, its residue modulo $p$ is~$1$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
For integers $b,n$, let
$C_b(n,k)=k![x^k](1-x)^{-n}\log((1-x)/(1-bx))$.
These are integers, and for $k\geq1$ and every prime $p$,
\[
 C_b(n,k)\equiv(k-1)!(b^k-1)\pmod k,\qquad
 C_b(n,p)\equiv1-b\pmod p.
\]
Every composite $k\ne4$ divides $C_b(n,k)$; a prime $p$ divides
$C_b(n,p)$ exactly when $p\mid b-1$; and $4\mid C_b(n,4)$
exactly when $b$ is odd.
The quotient $C_b(n,p)/(p-1)$ is integral for every $n$ if
$p=2$, $p\geq7$ or $b$ is odd. For even $b$ and $p=3,5$ it is
integral exactly when $n$ is even. Each integral quotient has
residue $b-1$ modulo $p$.

nodes.statement:
The negative-sum counts, namely A344608, satisfy
$N(m)\le N(m+1)$ for every $m\ge0$, answering its COMMENTS
monotonicity question \cite{a344608}.
The COMMENTS of A344743 say exactly ``Conjecture: a(n) >= A236914.''
\cite{a344743}, without specifying the argument on the right.
A common-index reading is not asserted explicitly in the source;
it fails at $n=1$, with sides $0$ and $1$.
A precise valid comparison is
\begin{equation}
 \mathrm{A344743}(n+1)\ \ge\ \mathrm{A236914}(n)
 \qquad(n\ge0).
\end{equation}
Equality in \eqref{eq:corrected} holds exactly for $n=0,1,2,3$;
for $n\ge4$ its deficit is at least $\lfloor(n-4)/2\rfloor+1$.
More generally, $N(m)=N(m+1)$ exactly for
$m\in\{0,1,3,5,7\}$.
By conjugation, $N(m)$ also counts partitions with even largest part
and at least one odd part. In particular, the odd-weight identity is
$N(2n+1)=E(2n+1)$; the index $2n+2$ and the phrase concerning parts
not all odd in the COMMENTS of A344608 require these corrections.

nodes.statement:
For $j\in\N$, $T(F_j)=F_{j+1}$. For $j\geq2$,
$(F_j-1)^4-1$ divides $2^{F_j-1}-1$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \varphi(F_j-2)=(F_j-1)/2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\leq j\leq5.
\end{equation}
In general this totient equality holds exactly when all $F_i$ with $i<j$
are prime. The implication from primality to this equality for every $j$
is therefore equivalent to the assertion that no Fermat prime has index
$j\geq6$.

nodes.statement:
For every $n,d\geq3$, define
\[
 T=d^2-3d+3,\quad
 w_*=-\frac{2d-3}{dT},\quad
 p_* =\frac{(d-2)^2}{Tk},\quad
 e_* =\frac1{(d-1)^3+1},\quad
 h=\frac1{d^2(d-2)},
\]
with $k$ as in \eqref{eq:rank}. Then $0<p_*<1$, $w(p_*)=w_*$, and
\begin{equation}
 \eps^{n,d}(p_*)=e_* < e_*+h p_*\left(1-\frac RM\right)
                  \leq \EG(\rho(p_*)).
\end{equation}
In particular, for $n=d=3$ one has $p_*=3/8$ and
\begin{equation}
 \eps^{3,3}(3/8)=\frac19=\frac{12}{108}
       <\frac{13}{108}\leq\EG(\rho_{3,3}(3/8)).
\end{equation}

Put
\[

M=\frac{21943673}{1280},\qquad \ab=\frac{5269}{10000}.
\]
For every real $a\geq\ac$,
\begin{equation}
G_a''(1/64)>M(a-\ac)\geq0.
\end{equation}
For every $a\geq\ab$ the stronger numerical margin is
\begin{equation}
G_a''(1/64)>\frac{26102771679}{22937600000}>1.

\end{equation}
Thus $-G_a$ is not completely monotone whenever $a\geq\ac$.
In particular,
$0<\ac<\ab<527/1000<155/294$, so \eqref{eq:claim} is false.

$\Theta:\mathsf L_d\to\mathsf L_d$ has completely positive Choi action

$\DIO_d$, even without requiring idempotence.

nodes.statement:
Let $a,b\geq1$, and consider channels on $M_a\otimes M_b$.
For either destruction $\mathcal D_a\otimes\id_b$ with $a\geq2$, or
$\Delta_a\otimes\id_b$ with $a\geq3$, any complex-linear transformation
with completely positive Choi action fixing every destruction-covariant
channel is the identity. Neither covariant class is an exact physical
fixed set. For $\Delta_a\otimes\id_b$, such a fixed-set projection exists
exactly when $a\leq2$.
In particular, the answer is negative for nonuniformity and conditional
nonuniformity in Table~I of Yoeli and Gour.

but
\[
 P(D_k)=P(D_{n-k})=P(A_t)\quad(0\leq t\leq1).
